paragraphs.text: OF ANASTASIUS OF SINAI, AMONG THE SAINTS: DISCOURSE ON THE HOLY SYNAXIS, AND [?] ON NOT JUDGING AND NOT BEARING GRUDGES. Through the whole of God's Scripture the grace of the Holy Spirit always urges us to carry out his divine commandments. It does so above all in the exhortation given through the prophet David, which is sung every day in the psalmody. For the book of Psalms teaches godliness and lays down the law about faith. It teaches self-control and leads us into the fear of God. It speaks of punishment, of compunction, of continence, of repentance, of compassion, of the love of God, of patience [toward?] God, of purity, of long-suffering, of fasting and of doing good. For constant attendance upon prayer and the divine Scriptures, and leisure given to them, is the mother of all the virtues. Through prayer we receive every request and every gift from God [?]. "In the assemblies," it says, "bless God," and, "In the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." This is why the Prophet, speaking as if in the person of God, necessarily

lays down for us unceasing attendance upon God and leisure for him, saying: "Be still and know that I am God." For without leisure and much perseverance in prayer and in the divine readings of the Scriptures, it is not possible either to receive what we ask for or truly [?] God

Someone in the schools of the perishable crafts often spends a good many years and can still barely learn an ordinary trade. How much more, then, ought anyone who wishes to come to the knowledge of God and to succeed in pleasing him to give his time to God, and to keep his soul warmly and fervently winged toward him until the end of his life? Do you not see those who take up worldly and temporary offices? Once they seize an opportunity, their own thoughts drive them and press them on as if fire were pushing them, and each of them says: "While I have the opportunity! While I hold power! While I can give orders and be obeyed! While the affairs of life obey me at once! I will grow rich, I will build, I will plant, I will seize, I will expand, I will get ahead before the times change. Let me not wait, let me not neglect it, for I do not know what the coming day will bring." Driven and pressed by these thoughts and others like them, as if by demons, most people hurry on, choked by temptations and worldly cares, and they bring nothing to maturity. They have not a word to say about the soul, about death, about punishment [?] or about judgment. We hardly know ourselves, and we deceive ourselves. If only this were all, the evil would be smaller. But we also hate one another, revile, plot, envy, slander and [?] mock. None of us pays attention to his own sins, and no one cares about his own burden. Instead we scrutinize our neighbors' sins closely while we are full of mire up to the neck, and we give no thought to that. Until old age we busy ourselves with other people's affairs, and not even in old age do we examine our own evils. We see the small faults of our brothers but do not see the beam in our own eye. We are bent double under the burden of our sins and pry into the faults of others. Even so we feel no shame. We spare no one and revere no one. We bite everyone and devour everyone: the small and the great, the guilty and the innocent, the priests, our teachers, those who guide us, those who admonish us and turn us back. This is why the wrath of God comes upon us. This is why we are chastised and handed over to many afflictions and calamities, because of the hardness of heart that holds us fast.
(2) "He necessarily lays down the [?] toward God": for [?] the attendance and leisure. COMBEFIS.

Great is our blindness, great our sloth, great our negligence. Among us there is no compunction, no fear of God, no amendment, no repentance. Our whole mind is given to wickedness, luxury and drunkenness. We often spend the whole day in theaters, in obscene talk and in the other works of the devil without growing weary. For these things we even neglect food, home and other necessary business. Yet in the church of God, at prayer and the reading, we are unwilling to stand before God for a single hour. We hurry out of the church of God as if fleeing a fire. If a longer passage of the divine Gospel is read, we grow irritated and distracted. If the priest saying the prayers draws them out a little, we sulk and lose heart. If the one offering the bloodless sacrifice is a little slow, we grow listless, sulking and yawning, and we are eager to get away from the prayer as quickly as from a law court. Then the devil hurries us off to vain pursuits and debauchery. Great indeed is our wretchedness, beloved. We ought to give ourselves fervently and intently to every prayer and supplication, and above all to the divine celebration of the immaculate mysteries. It is our duty to stand before the Master with fear and trembling at such a Synaxis. Yet we do not even offer it to him with sincere supplication and a broken and contrite mind. Instead we conduct our lawsuits and manage our many vain affairs during these Synaxes. Some take no thought for the purification and repentance with which they should approach the holy table, but only for the clothes in which they will adorn themselves. Others come but do not deign to stay until the end. They ask others what is happening in the Synaxis and whether the time for communion has come. Then they rush in at a run like dogs, snatch the mystical bread and leave. Others are present in the temple of God but cannot keep quiet for a single hour. They chatter with one another and are taken up with nonsense rather than prayer. Others abandon the mystagogy of the divine liturgy and give themselves over to the pleasures of the flesh. Others do not take the time to attend to their own conscience and cleanse themselves of the filth of (Note: Basil. and Combefis: "if he reads a passage." (5) "If you read a longer passage" [?])

their sins by recognizing them. Instead they pile heavier burdens of sin upon themselves by gazing at the beauty and the figures of women, and through their irrational lust they turn the church of God into a brothel. Others make deals about business and property, turning that most awe-inspiring hour into a place of commerce and a marketplace. Others busy themselves slandering one another, or even the priests themselves while they are offering the sacrifice in the Synaxis. Some of the women are not free of such things either. Besides these, the women who serve the devil frequent the church of God not so much for prayer as to be seen and to lead astray many of the simpler folk. Since my exhortation, then, takes in both sexes, men and women alike, I return to the course my discourse took at the start. I say these things in lament, for this is what our own sloth and contempt have done to us who seem to be Christians. What could be more terrible than behaving like this? We carry robberies, wickedness and a multitude of sins within us, wash our hands with a little water, and then, unclean and filthy as we are, take to ourselves that holy body and the divine blood poured out for the salvation of the world. Do you not see how Judas partook of the Master's body unworthily and deceitfully, was immediately condemned, and gave the evil one greater room? For it says: "And when he had taken the morsel, at once Satan entered into him." The devil did not despise the bread. He was exposing the one who partook, because he had partaken to his own condemnation. Tell me, with what conscience do you approach the mysteries? With what soul, with what thoughts, when you have your conscience within you as your accuser? Tell me, if you were carrying dung in your hands, would you have dared to touch the king's robes? But why do I say that? You would not even touch your own clothes with dirty hands. You would first wash and wipe them, and only then touch your clothes. Why, then, do you not offer God even the honor you give to cheap garments and clothing? Tell me, what pardon will you obtain? What pleases God is not entering the church of God, or kissing the divine images of the holy icons and the precious crosses. Nor is washing one's hands with water (Notes: 1. Canisius: "to Christ." 2. Canisius: "pleasing" [variant accent].)

the cleansing. The cleansing is to flee and wash away the filth of sins, to scour away the chains of sin with confession, tears and a humbled soul, and to approach the immaculate mysteries in that state. But perhaps someone will say: "It is not easy for me to weep and lament over myself." Why? Because you do not toil, because you do not feel, because you do not consider the fearful day of judgment. Still, if you cannot weep, at least groan painfully and be sorrowful. Cut off your laughter, or at least cast away your pride. Stand before the Master with fear, your eyes bowed to the ground, and confess to him with a lowly mind. Do you not see those who stand before an earthly king, often even an impious one? They stand before him with all reverence and with fear [?], their eyes fixed on him. They do not speak, they do not move, they are not distracted, but stand before him in quiet and fear. We, on the other hand, stand in the church of God as if in a theater or a bathhouse. We laugh, babble and chatter, deceiving ourselves into thinking that we are standing in church. Do you not know that the church of God is a hospital and a harbor? If you stay sick in the hospital and receive no treatment, when will you ever be healed? And if you are tossed by storms in the harbor, where will you ever find calm? Stand with reverence, I implore you. Stand with fear in the fearful hour of the anaphora. Whatever disposition and thoughts each of you has as he stands there at that hour, in that state he too is offered up to the Master. It is called the anaphora, the "offering up," because it is offered up to God. Stand before God, then, in quiet and compunction. Confess your sins to God through the priests. Condemn your deeds and do not be ashamed. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace. Condemn yourself before men, so that the Judge may justify you before the angels and the whole world. Ask for mercy, ask for pardon, ask for forgiveness of past sins and deliverance from those to come. Then you may approach the mysteries fittingly and partake of the body and the blood with a pure conscience, and they will be for your cleansing and not for your condemnation. Hear the divine Paul saying: "Let each one examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup.

For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. That is why many among you are weak and sick, and quite a few have fallen asleep." Do you see that sickness and death are, for the most part, brought on by approaching the divine mysteries unworthily? But perhaps you will say: "And who is worthy?" I know that too. Yet you will become worthy, if only you are willing. Recognize that you are a sinner. Cut yourself off from sin. Turn away from sin, from wickedness and from anger. Show the works of repentance. Take up self-control, gentleness and long-suffering. Show compassion to those in need from the fruits of righteousness, and you have become worthy. Pray to God with a contrite soul, and he will fulfill your requests. If you do not do this, you spend your time in church in vain. The word is not mine; it is the Master's voice: "Why," he says, "do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and do not do my will?" Indeed, faith without works is dead. "What then?" someone says. "Since my works are evil, ought I not to pray? Ought I not to spend time in the church [?] of God?" That is not what I say, nor do I permit it. What I urge is that we pray as we ought, so that when we come to prayer we may stand in a manner worthy of God. Otherwise Christ may say to us also what he said to the Jews: "My house shall be called a house of prayer,"

The Lord beat those who sold and bought in the Jewish temple and drove them out. If that was their fate, what punishment and what Gehenna will be judged fitting for those who revile one another and bear grudges? And what shall we suffer, who are enrolled under God yet submit to the devil? The priest is a mediator between God and men, and he propitiates God for the forgiveness [?] of the sins of the people. See, then, how he puts everyone on guard beforehand and solemnly warns them, as if he were saying something like this to the people: "Men, since you have set me up at this mystical table as your mediator before God, I beg you, strive along with me. Withdraw from all worldly thoughts. Leave behind every bodily care, for this is the time for earnest prayer, not for vain business. Hear what the deacon calls out to you: [?]

[?] our necks, let us close the mind [?], let us close the tongue, let us fill [?] the mind, let us ascend to heaven. Let us hold our minds and hearts on high. Let us lift the eye of the soul up to God. Let us pass beyond heaven, beyond the angels, beyond the Cherubim, and run to the Master's very throne. Let us take hold of the immaculate feet of Christ himself. Let us weep, let us do violence to his compassion, let us confess at his holy, heavenly and spiritual altar." This is the solemn charge the priest gives us when he says: "Let us lift up our hearts." And what do we answer? "We have them with the Lord." What are you saying? What are you doing? Your mind is hovering over perishable and temporary things, busy with appearances, possessions, pleasures and lawsuits, and you say, "I have it with the Lord"? Take care, I beg you, that your mind is not below with the devil instead of above with the Lord. What are you doing, man? The priest is offering the bloodless sacrifice to the Master on your behalf, and you show contempt? The priest is contending for you. He stands at the altar as before a fearful tribunal, entreating and pressing that the grace of the Holy Spirit may come down upon you from above, and you take no care for your own salvation? No, I beg you. Abandon this evil and vain habit. Cry out together with the priest who contends for you; labor with him as he prays for you. Give yourself to the work of your own salvation. "The prayer of a righteous man, when it is effective, has great power." It is effective if you too contend alongside the priest and show the fruits of repentance. For if one builds and another tears down, what have they gained but toil? And what terror is lacking in this tearing down [?]? Not only do we lie to Christ at that fearful hour of the divine Synaxis, but we also bear grudges against our own brothers while saying in the prayer: "And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."
VARIANT READINGS. 1. Canisius: "the mind." 2. Combefis: "For what is worse than this tearing down?"

What are you saying, man? Why do you behave so boldly and insolently toward God? You bear a grudge against your brother. You are sharpening a sword against him, devising snares against him, carrying evil venom in your heart, and yet you cry to God: "Forgive me my debts, as I too have forgiven my debtor"? Did you come to the church of God to pray, or to lie? To receive grace, or to draw down wrath? To obtain forgiveness of sins, or to add to your offenses? To carry off salvation, or punishment? Do you not see that this is why we greet one another at that fearful hour? It is so that we may cast off every bond of injustice and hardness of heart and approach the Master with a pure heart. What are you doing, man? The angels are ministering. The six-winged ones are covering the mystical table. The Cherubim stand by and cry out the thrice-holy hymn with radiant voice, and the Seraphim bow down in reverence. The high priest is making propitiation for you, and all are disposed [?] in fear and trembling. The Lamb of God is being sacrificed, and the Holy Spirit is coming down from above. Angels are moving invisibly among all the people, marking and recording the souls of the faithful. And at such a time, do you not shudder at your own contempt? You greet your brother with a Jewish kiss, while you hide long-standing grudges against him in your heart, and the deadly [venom] of the serpent. How can you not shudder and fall down as you say to him who knows the secrets of the heart, "Forgive me as I too have forgiven my brother"? How does such a prayer of yours differ from a curse? See, what you say, you pronounce against yourself: "If I forgive, forgive me. If I pardon, pardon me. If I have compassion, have compassion on me. If I hold a grudge against my fellow servant, hold one against me. If I am angry, be angry with me. With the measure I measure, let it be measured to me. If I pardon in hypocrisy, let me be shown mercy in hypocrisy. I pass sentence against myself, Master. For I have heard your fearful voice saying: 'With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you.' And: 'If you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you.' Persuaded, then, by the decrees of these [?] words of yours, I have forgiven and pardoned those who have wronged me;

so forgive me, Master, as I too have forgiven my fellow servants." Let us say these things. Let us pray them every day as we stand at the time of the fearful and awesome Synaxis. Knowing this, the priest raises the bread of life after that bloodless sacrifice has been sanctified and shows it to everyone. Then the deacon [?] and says: "Let us attend," that is, "Take heed to yourselves, brothers." It is as if he said: "Look, a little while ago you declared, 'We have our hearts with the Lord.' And again, confessing to God that you were pure and free of grudges, you said, 'Forgive us, as we also forgive our debtors,' and you greeted one another. But I too am only a man and do not know your thoughts, so I put the judgment away from myself. I do not know who is worthy or unworthy to partake of these mysteries. That is why I call on you to take heed to yourselves and to recognize before whom you stand." Then the priest immediately adds: "The holy things for the holy." And what does he mean? "See, beloved, how you approach the partaking of the divine mysteries. Let none of you, coming forward to partake, hear the words: 'Do not touch me; depart from me, you who practice grudge-bearing and lawlessness.' Go far away, you who have not forgiven your brother. Then come and offer your gift, and you will be counted worthy to partake. Cast away from yourself all the mire of wickedness, and then come and receive the purifying coal. Say to him: 'I know, Master, that I owe many sins and debts. But because of your commandment I have forgiven my brothers, so that I too may be counted worthy of forgiveness from you, Master.'" These things and others like them are what the priest suggests to us through that short exclamation. Therefore let us forgive our brothers and cast away from ourselves all malice and wickedness, we who wish to walk worthily of the calling to which we were called. Do not say, "I have forgiven my brother many times, and he has sinned against me again," for you will hear the same from the Master. Do not say, "So-and-so has wronged me greatly. He plotted against my house, he seized my field, he killed my son, he did me much harm, he threw me into prison, he handed me over to death, and I cannot forgive this." No, beloved, do not speak like that, I beg you. For however much you forgive your brother, the Master will forgive you as much and more. Imitate Stephen too, the first among the martyrs. What did he say as he was being stoned? "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." Imitate James the brother of God, whose also [?]

[?] whom the chroniclers (15) record praying for those who were putting him to death, and saying, “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Imitate the Master himself, who accepted death for your salvation; and even if your brother wants to hang you on a tree, cry out together with the Master and say, “Father, forgive them this sin.” Look at the man who owed the Master ten thousand talents. When you hear “ten thousand talents,” understand loads of sins. Because he fell down before the Master, because he begged him, because he moved him to pity, he obtained pardon for all those debts. But when he held a grudge and would not pardon his fellow servant, he found no more relief. Instead he was handed over to eternal Gehenna, and his grudge alone was enough to destroy him, more than all those heavy sins of the ten thousand talents. So, I beg you, let us flee this wicked and unpardonable sin. And if you want to learn that the darkness of resentment is worse than any other sin, listen. Every other sin is committed in a short time and quickly comes to an end. Someone commits fornication, for example, and afterward, realizing how great the sin is, he comes to acknowledge it. But resentment keeps its passion inflamed without pause. For whether he is getting up or lying down, praying or walking along the road, the one held by this passion carries its venom in his heart without pause or respite, so that whoever is enslaved to it neither enjoys the grace of God nor is counted worthy of the forgiveness of sins. For where resentment has taken root, nothing is of any use: not fasting, not prayer, not tears, not confession, not supplication, not virginity, not almsgiving, not any other good thing. Resentment against one's brother undoes them all. Let us also pay careful attention to this: he did not say, “If you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that you have something against your brother,” but, “and remember that your brother has something against you, go first, be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” If, then, we are obliged to heal even our brother's malice and wickedness, what excuse do we have

when we not only fail to do this but even hold grudges against our brothers, and hide the [?] venom of the serpent within ourselves? I often hear many people saying, “Alas, how can I be saved? I am not strong enough to fast, I do not know how to keep vigil, I cannot remain a virgin, I cannot bear to withdraw from the world. How then can I be saved?” How? [?] I tell you: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; pardon, and you will be pardoned.” There is one short road to salvation. Let me show you a second as well. Which? “Do not judge,” he says, “and you will not be judged.” Here is another, without fasting or vigils or toil. So do not judge your brother, even if you see him sinning with your own eyes. For there is one Judge and Master, who will repay each according to his works, and one day of judgment, on which we shall stand laid bare according to our deeds and receive God's mercy. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” So whoever judges before the coming of Christ is an Antichrist, because he seizes the dignity that belongs to Christ. Let us not judge our brothers, then, I beg you, so that we may [?] obtain pardon. You may perhaps see him sinning, but you do not know what kind of end his life will come to. The thief who was crucified with Jesus was a murderer and a killer of men, while Judas was an apostle and a disciple of Jesus, one of his genuine disciples; yet in a short [?] time the exchange took place: the thief went to the kingdom, and the disciple to perdition. But suppose your brother is indeed a sinner: how do you know the rest of his deeds? For many people have often sinned openly and repented greatly in secret. We saw them sinning, but we did not know of their repentance and [?]; in our eyes they are judged as sinners, but before God they are justified. So, I beg you, let us not hold grudges, and let us not judge anyone at all, until the just Judge comes,

who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts. Above all (17), do not sit in judgment on a priest of God about hidden and uncertain matters you have heard concerning him. Do not say, “The one making the offering is a sinner, he stands condemned, he is unworthy, and the grace of the all-holy Spirit does not come down.” Do not entertain any such thought. There is Another who knows and examines hidden things. Know yourself, that everyone is [?] than you, and leave judgment to the just Judge. Provided the priest does not err in the doctrines concerning God, you are no judge of the rest, unless indeed you have lost your senses; you should recognize your own measure and rank. “What then?” someone says. “Is he not subject to examination and to the canons of the Church [?]?” Yes, I say. But he will not be examined by you; he will be examined by God, or often by a higher bishop. Why do you, a sheep, examine the shepherd? Why do you, like a Pharisee, seize God's judgment seat and the sacred dignity, which was not entrusted to you and has not been committed to you by God? So, I beg you, do not judge anyone, and above all not a priest of God. Instead, come to the divine mysteries with faith, with repentance shown in deeds, and with a clean conscience, and you will obtain sanctification in everything. For even if the one offering the bloodless sacrifice is an angel of God, if you come unworthily, the angel will by no means cleanse you of your sins. That this saying is true, Judas himself bears witness. He received the divine bread from the Master's own spotless hands, but because he received it unworthily, Satan immediately entered into him. And if you want to hear a story showing that not judging anyone sets us free from our sins, and

that judging, on the other hand, seals them, listen. For, as Christ our Master is my witness, those who saw this are still living in the flesh. There was a man, one of those who wore the monastic habit, who spent his life in complete negligence and laziness. He fell ill with his last illness, and when he came to his final breaths, he was not at all afraid of his death, but parted from his body with complete thankfulness and eagerness. So one of the most God-loving fathers sitting with him asked him, “Brother, believe us: from what we observed, we supposed that you spent your life in complete laziness and negligence, and we do not know where such freedom from care at this hour comes from.” To this the brother replied, “Truly, honored fathers, I really did spend my life in complete laziness. And just now, at this hour, the angels of God brought me the record of my sins, and after reading out the sins I had committed ever since I renounced the world, they said to me, ‘Do you recognize these?’ And I said, ‘Yes, I know them exactly. Yet ever since I renounced the world and became a monk, I have neither judged any human being nor held a grudge. And I ask that Christ's word be kept in my case too. For he said, “Do not judge, and you will not be judged,” and, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”’ And as soon as I had said this to the angels, the record of my sins was torn up at once. And look, I am departing to Christ with great joy and freedom from care.” And when the brother had told this to the fathers, he gave up his spirit to the Lord in peace, having brought every benefit and edification to those who stood around him. May we too be counted worthy of that benefit, edification and portion, by keeping ourselves unwounded by all condemnation and resentment, through the grace and love for mankind of our all-holy and merciful God; for to him belongs all glory, [?] and worship, with his only-begotten Son and his all-holy and [?] Spirit, now and ever, and to the ages of ages. Amen. [?] seals. [?]
